questions.question:
An algorithm has to store several keys generated by an adversary in a hash table. The adversary is malicious who tries to maximize the number of collisions. Let [latex] k[/latex] be the number of keys, [latex] m[/latex] be the number of slots in the hash table, and [latex] k \gt m[/latex].
Which one of the following is the best hashing strategy to counteract the adversary?

options.A: Division method, i.e., use the hash function [latex]h(k) = k\;  mod \; m[/latex]
options.B:
Multiplication method, i.e., use the hash function [latex] h(k) =  \left \lfloor m(kA -\left \lfloor kA \right \rfloor ) \right \rfloor[/latex], where
[latex]A[/latex] is a carefully chosen constant.
options.D: If [latex]k[/latex] is a prime number, use Division method. Otherwise, use Multiplication method

questions.explanation:
Any fixed hash function (division or multiplication) is known to the adversary, who can pick keys that all collide.

Universal hashing picks the hash function at random from a family at run time, so the adversary cannot predict it, and the expected number of collisions stays small.

Answer: Universal hashing method

[latex]a="@\#Hello\ World!"[/latex] occupies indices [latex]0[/latex]-[latex]14[/latex] (`@`,`#`,`H`,`e`,`l`,`l`,`o`,` `,`W`,`o`,`r`,`l`,`d`,`!`,`\0`). [latex]\text{stringcopy(a, a+2)}[/latex] sets [latex]s=a[/latex] (index [latex]0[/latex]) and [latex]t=a+2[/latex] (index [latex]2[/latex]), copying forward while [latex]{*}t[/latex] is non-null (checked before each copy).

Since the loop condition is checked before copying, it copies indices [latex]2[/latex] through [latex]13[/latex] (`H` through `!`, [latex]12[/latex] characters) into destination indices [latex]0[/latex] through [latex]11[/latex], then stops as soon as [latex]{*}t[/latex] hits the original null at index [latex]14[/latex] — without ever writing a new null terminator into the destination.

So after the copy: indices [latex]0[/latex]-[latex]11[/latex] hold the shifted text `Hello World!`, but indices [latex]12,13,14[/latex] still hold their original, untouched values: `d`, `!`, and the original `\0`.

[latex]\text{printf("\%s")}[/latex] prints from index [latex]0[/latex] until it hits the first null — which is still the original one at index [latex]14[/latex]. So it prints: `Hello World!` (indices 0-11) followed by the leftover `d` (index 12) and `!` (index 13) before finally stopping at the null.

Answer: Hello World!d!

questions.question: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree (BST) having [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers?

options.A: The maximum length of a path from the root node to any other node is [latex](n - 1)[/latex].
options.B: An inorder traversal will always produce a sorted sequence of elements.
options.C: Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2 n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
options.D: Every BST is also a Min-Heap.

questions.explanation:
Checking each BST claim for [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers:

- Maximum path length from root to any node is [latex]n-1[/latex]: true — in the worst case (a completely skewed/degenerate BST, essentially a linked list), all [latex]n[/latex] nodes form a single chain, giving a root-to-deepest-node path of [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, which is also the largest this can ever be since there are only [latex]n[/latex] nodes total.
- Inorder traversal always produces sorted order: true — this is the defining property of a BST (left subtree [latex]<[/latex] node [latex]<[/latex] right subtree, recursively), and it holds regardless of the tree's shape.
- Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2n)[/latex] time in the worst case: false — that bound only holds for a balanced BST. A skewed/degenerate BST (as noted above) can force search time all the way up to [latex]O(n)[/latex].
- Every BST is also a Min-Heap: false — a min-heap requires every parent to be smaller than both children, but a BST only orders left [latex]<[/latex] parent [latex]<[/latex] right; nothing stops a BST's left child from being smaller than its grandparent in ways that violate heap order.

Answer: Max path length is n-1; and inorder traversal always gives sorted order.

Finding the maximum of 512 elements needs 512 [latex]-[/latex] 1 = 511 comparisons.

Answer: 511

questions.question:
The following sequence corresponds to the preorder traversal of a binary search tree [latex]T[/latex] :

[latex] 50,25,13,40,30,47,75,60,70,80,77 [/latex]

The position of the element [latex]60[/latex] in the postorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] is ________ . (answer in integer)
Note: The position begins with [latex]1[/latex].
questions.explanation:
Reconstruct the BST from the preorder [latex]50,25,13,40,30,47,75,60,70,80,77[/latex] (each root's left subtree holds smaller values, right subtree holds larger values, read off in preorder root-first fashion):

[latex]50[/latex] is the root. Left subtree (values [latex]<50[/latex]): [latex]25,13,40,30,47[/latex]; right subtree (values [latex]>50[/latex]): [latex]75,60,70,80,77[/latex].
Left subtree: root [latex]25[/latex], left child [latex]13[/latex] (leaf), right subtree [latex]40,30,47[/latex] → root [latex]40[/latex], left [latex]30[/latex], right [latex]47[/latex].
Right subtree: root [latex]75[/latex], left subtree [latex]60,70[/latex] → root [latex]60[/latex] with right child [latex]70[/latex] (no left); right subtree [latex]80,77[/latex] → root [latex]80[/latex] with left child [latex]77[/latex] (no right).

Postorder (left, right, root) of the whole tree:
From the [latex]25[/latex]-subtree: [latex]13,\ 30,47,40,\ 25[/latex]
From the [latex]75[/latex]-subtree: [latex]70,60,\ 77,80,\ 75[/latex]
Then the root [latex]50[/latex].

Full postorder: [latex]13,\,30,\,47,\,40,\,25,\,70,\,60,\,77,\,80,\,75,\,50[/latex]

Counting positions (starting at [latex]1[/latex]): [latex]60[/latex] is the [latex]7[/latex]th element.

Answer: 7

questions.question: Suppose we have a balanced binary search tree T holding n numbers. We are given two numbers L and H and wish to sum up all the numbers in T that lie between L and H. Suppose there are m such numbers in T. If the tightest upper bound on the time to compute the sum is [latex]O(n^{a}log^{b}n+m^{c}log^{d}n)[/latex], the value of a + 10b + 100c + 1000d is _______.
questions.explanation:
Find L in the balanced BST in [latex]O(\log n)[/latex], then walk in-order through the m values up to H in O(m).

Time = [latex]O(\log n+m)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] a = 0, b = 1, c = 1, d = 0

a + 10b + 100c + 1000d = 0 + 10 + 100 + 0 = 110

Answer: 110

questions.question: An operator delete(i) for a binary heap data structure is to be designed to delete the item in the i-th node.Assume that the heap is implemented in an array and i refers to the i-th index of thearray.If the heap tree has depth d (number of edges on the path from the root to the farthest leaf),the n what is the time complexity to re-fix the heap efficiently after the removal of the element?
questions.explanation:
To delete node i: move the last element into position i, then either sift it up or down. Either way it moves along one root-to-leaf path, at most d levels [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(d)[/latex]. It can take that long, so it is not [latex]O(1)[/latex].

Answer: O(d) but not O(1)
